longest-common-prefix.pattern: Character-by-character comparison (vertical scan); a trie generalises it

approaches.name: Horizontal scan: shrink the prefix word by word
approaches.idea: Start with the first word as the candidate prefix. For each next word, cut the candidate back until the word starts with it.
steps: Set `prefix = strs[0]`.
For each other word, while it does not start with `prefix`, drop the last character of `prefix`.
Return `prefix` (possibly empty).
approaches.why: S is the total number of characters: each comparison is bounded by the word length, and the prefix only shrinks. It still compares whole prefixes for every word even if the first word is long.

approaches.name: Vertical scan: compare column by column
approaches.idea: Check position 0 of every word, then position 1, and so on. Stop at the first position where some word ends or disagrees with the first word.
steps: For each index `i` of the first word:
If any word has length `i` or a different character at `i`, return `strs[0][0..i)`.
If the loop finishes, the whole first word is the prefix.
approaches.why: n words × (m + 1) positions, where m is the answer's length: it never reads past the first mismatch.

implement-trie-prefix-tree.pattern: Trie: one node per prefix, children indexed by letter, an end-of-word flag

approaches.name: A set of words, scanning it for prefixes
approaches.idea: Store every inserted word in a hash set. Exact search is a set lookup; `startsWith` checks every stored word.
steps: `insert`: add the word to the set.
`search`: return whether the set contains it.
`startsWith`: return whether any word in the set starts with the prefix.
approaches.why: `insert` and `search` cost O(L) to hash the word, but `startsWith` scans all N words. Storage is every word in full.

approaches.name: Trie of 26-way nodes
approaches.idea: Each node represents a prefix and has up to 26 children, one per next letter; a flag marks nodes where a full word ends. Every operation walks one path of length L.
steps: `insert`: from the root, follow (creating if missing) the child for each letter; mark the last node as a word end.
`search`: follow the letters; fail on a missing child; succeed only if the last node is a word end.
`startsWith`: follow the letters; succeed if the walk completes.
approaches.why: Each call touches one node per character. T is the total number of trie nodes (at most the total length of inserted words), each with 26 child slots.

design-add-and-search-words-data-structu.pattern: Trie + DFS that branches on wildcards

approaches.name: Compare the pattern with every stored word
approaches.idea: Keep a list of words. A pattern matches a word of the same length if every non-dot character is equal.
steps: `addWord`: append to the list.
`search`: for each stored word of the same length, compare position by position (a `.` matches anything); return true on the first match.
approaches.why: Every search looks at all N words of up to L letters.

approaches.name: Trie with DFS on dots
approaches.idea: Store the words in a trie. Searching follows a single child for each letter; a `.` tries every existing child. The trie shares prefixes, so most branches die out quickly.
steps: `addWord`: insert into the trie and mark the end node.
`search(node, i)`: if `i == word.length`, return whether `node` ends a word.
If `word[i]` is a letter, continue in that child (fail if missing); if it is `.`, return true if any child succeeds.
approaches.why: With d dots (at most 2 here) a search explores up to 26ᵈ branches of length L; without dots it is a single O(L) path. T is the number of trie nodes.

replace-words.pattern: Trie of roots; for each word, walk until the first root ends

approaches.name: Try every root against every word
approaches.idea: For each word in the sentence, check every root; among the roots the word starts with, keep the shortest.
steps: Split the sentence into words.
For each word, scan all roots and keep the shortest one the word starts with.
Replace the word with it (if any) and join the words with spaces.
approaches.why: W words × D roots, each prefix check up to L characters. The split words take O(n) for a sentence of n characters.

approaches.name: Hash set of roots, try each prefix length
approaches.idea: Put the roots in a set. For each word, test its prefixes from shortest to longest; the first one in the set is the shortest root.
steps: Add all roots to a hash set.
For each word, for `len = 1 .. word.length`, if `word[0..len)` is in the set, use it and stop.
Join the results with spaces.
approaches.why: Each word tries up to L prefixes, and building/hashing each prefix costs O(L). No dependence on the number of roots per lookup.

approaches.name: Trie of roots
approaches.idea: Insert the roots into a trie. For each word, walk the trie letter by letter; the first node that ends a root gives the shortest root. If the walk breaks off first, keep the word.
steps: Insert every root into a trie, marking end nodes.
For each word, walk from the trie root; if a node marks a root end, replace the word with the prefix walked so far.
If a letter has no child, stop and keep the word. Join with spaces.
approaches.why: Building the trie costs the total root length; each character of the sentence is looked at at most once. The trie has at most D·L nodes.

search-suggestions-system.pattern: Sort + binary search on each prefix (or a trie that stores the top 3 per node)

approaches.name: Filter and sort for every typed prefix
approaches.idea: After each character, collect every product with that prefix, sort them, and keep the first three.
steps: For each prefix `searchWord[0..i]`:
Collect the products that start with it, sort them, and take up to three.
Append that list to the answer.
approaches.why: m prefixes; each filters n products (O(L) per check) and sorts the matches. The match list can hold n products.

approaches.name: Sort once, binary search each prefix
approaches.idea: In sorted order, all products with a given prefix form one contiguous block, starting at the first product `>=` the prefix. Binary search that position and take up to three products from there that still have the prefix.
steps: Sort `products`.
For each prefix, binary search the first index `i` with `products[i] >= prefix`.
Take `products[i], products[i + 1], products[i + 2]` while they exist and start with the prefix.
approaches.time: O(n log n·L + m·L log n)
approaches.why: One sort (string comparisons cost up to O(L)), then one binary search of O(log n) comparisons per typed character (the answer itself aside).

approaches.name: Trie keeping the first three words at each node
approaches.idea: Insert the products in sorted order into a trie, and let every node remember the first three products that pass through it. Typing then just walks down the trie, reading each node's list.
steps: Sort `products`. Insert each one; at every node on its path, append it to the node's list if the list has fewer than 3 entries.
Walk the trie along `searchWord`; after each character, output the current node's list.
Once a character has no child, output empty lists for the rest.
approaches.why: S is the total length of all products: building the trie is linear in it, and each typed character is O(1) plus copying three words. Memory is the trie itself.

maximum-xor-of-two-numbers-in-an-array.pattern: Binary trie of bits, greedily choosing the opposite bit from the top

approaches.name: XOR every pair
approaches.idea: Compute `nums[i] ^ nums[j]` for every pair and keep the largest.
steps: Set `best = 0`.
For every `i <= j`, update `best` with `nums[i] ^ nums[j]`.
Return `best`.

approaches.name: Binary trie, opposite bit first
approaches.idea: A higher bit is worth more than all lower bits together, so for each number choose, from bit 30 down, the partner bit that differs from its own whenever some stored number has it. Store the numbers in a trie keyed by bits (highest first) to make that choice in O(1) per bit.
steps: Insert every number into a binary trie, bit 30 first.
For each number `x`, walk the trie from the top: at bit `b`, prefer the child for `1 − bit(x, b)`; if it exists, add `1 << b` to the XOR and go there, else take the other child.
The best XOR over all `x` is the answer.
approaches.why: Each insert and each query walks 31 levels. The trie has at most 31 nodes per number.

word-search-ii.pattern: Trie of the words + DFS backtracking on the grid, pruning when no word has the current prefix

approaches.name: Run Word Search separately for every word
approaches.idea: For each word, try every starting cell and do a backtracking DFS that matches the word letter by letter, marking cells as used.
steps: For each word, for each cell: DFS(cell, index 0).
DFS: fail if out of bounds, used, or the letter differs; succeed at the last letter; otherwise mark the cell, try the 4 neighbours with the next index, and unmark.
Collect the words that were found.
approaches.why: Every word repeats the full grid search: from each of the m·n cells, up to 4·3ᴸ⁻¹ paths of length L. With 3 × 10⁴ words that is far too slow.

approaches.name: One grid DFS guided by a trie of all words
approaches.idea: Put all the words in a trie and search the grid once. The DFS carries the trie node for the letters walked so far; if the next letter has no child, no word continues that way, so the path is cut immediately. A node that ends a word records it; clearing that mark avoids reporting it twice.
steps: Insert every word into a trie; store the word itself at its end node.
From every cell, DFS with the trie root: move to the child for the cell's letter (stop if missing).
If that node holds a word, add it to the answer and clear it.
Mark the cell used, explore the 4 neighbours, then restore the cell.
approaches.why: The grid is searched once for all words together, and the trie prunes every path that is not a prefix of some word. S is the total length of the words (trie size); the recursion is at most L = 10 deep.
